newsitem.title: CHINA: China B share interim results seen improved.
newsitem.headline: China B share interim results seen improved.

text.p: China's foreign currency B share firms are expected to report improved first-half 1997 interim results, but the positive news might not be enough to drag the markets out of their summer slump, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Last year's interim results were horrendous, and on an overall basis most of the B-share companies are looking better," said Hoong Yik Luen, head of China research for ING Barings Securities in Shanghai.
"Profits of most listed companies are going to look bad, but they are not going to look as bad as last year," added a broker at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai.
Despite an expected improvement in interim results -- most of which will be announced in August -- the positive news would not be enough to drag the market out of the summer doldrums, analysts said.
Investors would selectively buy firms that stood out from the crowd, which is unlikely to lift the overall market, they said.

Two interest rate cuts last year, which reduced the cost of borrowing, and the current positive economic environment of steady growth and low inflation would help results improve this year, analysts said.
"I think we'll probably see more positive surprises than less because the economy has been expanding for the past year," said another foreign broker in Shanghai.
However, a recent government crackdown on listed firms speculating on the stock markets, previously a major source of investment income for public companies, could hurt earnings, analysts said.
"We will probably not see too much growth in interim results as the government has clamped down on excessive investment income," said an analyst at a foreign investment bank in Shenzhen.

Brokers were unwilling to predict which sectors would shine during results season but said certain companies looked troubled, including some producers of consumer goods, due to high costs and keen competition.
"It's a capacity problem -- too many people have come into the market for some types of consumer goods," said a foreign broker.
Other sectors would have winners and losers depending on the quality of management, analysts said.

But predicting interim results was tricky, they said, and warned against giving too much weight to the figures since most were only subject to a review, not the more stringent audit given to year-end results.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the top market watchdog, recently issued new rules on the drafting and publishing of interim reports in a bid to tighten supervision.

Accountants should audit the interim reports of companies that have suffered losses for two consecutive years, plan new share issues or aim to implement an interim dividend plan, official media have said.
"This (the CSRC move) is another step towards making the procedures in China the same as elsewhere," said Stuart Smith, managing partner of accountants Coopers & Lybrand in Shanghai.
"There's been a general concern that information isn't being released to shareholders as much as it should be," he said.
Poor disclosure by listed companies means there could be some surprises from B share firms during the upcoming reporting season as they suddenly made their business activities known, analysts said.
